Gawain. Sir Gawain stands as one of Arthur's most formidable and loyal knights, celebrated for strength that waxes and wanes with the sun. His confrontation with the mysterious Green Knight remains one of medieval literature's greatest tests of honor, courage, and the moral ambiguities underlying chivalric virtue.

Gawain was Arthur's nephew, often portrayed as his heir or champion in matters of the Crown's honor. He possessed supernatural strength that increased as the sun climbed toward noon and diminished toward evening, a power that defined many of his victories. He is the star of the tale Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, where he accepts a beheading challenge from an otherworldly opponent. He accepted the Green Knight's challenge to prove his courage, traveling to a mystical castle and ultimately learning hard lessons about temptation and honor.

He was known for courtesy and grace as well as martial prowess, embodying the ideal of the complete knight. Gawain remained fiercely loyal to Arthur even when other knights turned against the king, particularly in the final conflicts. He represents the tension between supernatural gifts, human weakness, and the genuine heroism required to maintain honor despite temptation. His connections run deep: King Arthur, his uncle and liege lord; the Green Knight, his otherworldly challenger and teacher in the virtue of honesty; and the Round Table, the fellowship of which he was a cornerstone.
